content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper uses synthetic CIFAR-like datasets to study the importance of invariance and equivariance in representation learning.

The main conclusion is that one needs the right amount of invariance: too much is bad, and to little is bad, too.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
While the paper is relatively easy to follow and investigates a number of different aspects / properties, my main concern is that the results are often close to common sense / trivial. A large body of work is concerned with learning the right types of invariance (for an overview see e.g. the related work section of "Group Equivariant Convolutional Networks" by Cohen et al. ICML 2016); the fact that one needs enough invariance is widely appreciated in the field while on the other hand the fact that too much invariance is harmful is also known. One of the most compelling demonstrations of this "too much invariance" phenomenon can be found in the paper "Excessive invariance causes adversarial vulnerability" (Jacobsen et al., ICLR 2019) which is not cited. (In terms of too much invariance is harmful, one might also consider the extreme case of a model with constant output, which is invariant towards all features: clearly, too much invariance is harmful). At points, the paper reads as if the authors are the first to think about certain topics: for instance by sentences like "So far, we have shown that invariances are important properties of representations".

Given that the importance of understanding the right degree of invariance/equivariance is already appreciated by the field, a very important _open_ question is how to learn them, most importantly which types of datasets require which types of invariances and equivariances. To this end, the experiments conducted on synthetic CIFAR-like data unfortunately don't allow many insights: while the authors "are interested in understanding how important invariances are for downstream applications", hardly anyone is using CIFAR training for downstream applications. In fact, if we already know which types of features are useful a priory (by design, via constructing synthetic datasets), then this becomes a very different problem compared to the common setting that we have a real-world dataset and would like to know which types of invariances our model should learn (which can be encouraged via e.g. data augmentation, architecture design, etc.).

In the light of this, **I don't think the experiments constitute a major advance over the existing state of knowledge.**

### Suggestions for improvement
In order to convince readers (and myself) otherwise, I would encourage the authors to apply/transfer their findings towards a non-toy problem for which the right answers (e.g. how much invariance to a certain feature is optimal) is not known in advance, and to show how the insights gained from the synthetic experiments transfer into measurable performance improvements under a realistic setting.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity, quality, novelty: see above.

Reproducibility: The paper uses error bars and averaged runs throughout the paper, which reduces variance and improves reliability. The paper provides details on experiments in the appendix, and I would like to point out that it includes the code to reproduce the findings itself in the supplementary data, which is laudable.

### MISC
- page 3: "some non-constant effect u": suggesting to be more precise here
- page 9 typo "highlights the need to ..."
content.summary_of_the_review: The experiments do not sufficiently advance the state of knowledge. I recommend rejection.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.title: Thank you for your valuable feedback! We will include the suggestions in a future version of the paper.
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful feedback and helpful suggestions! We will revise the paper to address the concerns that were raised.

### Highlighting novel results and connection to prior work
The reviewer rightfully points out a number of existing works exploring learning in- and equivariant representations as well as the implications of invariance and we will include them in the discussion of related work. We believe that highlighting the relative importance of invariance compared to other factors when transferring representations is a novel contribution of our work to this domain, but that we need to improve the clarity of the paper in this regard.

### Usefulness of the results for real-world problems
We agree with the reviewer that better understanding which invariances are useful for which downstream task is an important unsolved problem. However, the objectives of this work are somewhat orthogonal to this line of research. We want to mainly understand the relative importance of invariance compared to other factors. To do this, we need a setting where we already know which transformations are acting on inputs and which invariances are therefore required. This is not possible with typical real-world datasets. We will improve the clarity of the paper in this respect.
The suggestion of validating the conclusions derived from synthetic datasets on larger real-world tasks, however, is very valid and we will think about experiments that we can conduct in this regard.

Please also see our general comment for other issues that we are planning to address based on the feedback here.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors introduce Transforms-2D, a synthetic dataset that allows them to more precisely understand the changes in input from train to test.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
*Strength
I appreciate the effort to provide a dataset where transformations are well defined and models can be evaluated on.
*Weaknesses:
1) The authors make it seem as if invariance and equivariance is an arbitrary model choice and that we have no insights on why they are good. For instance, SSL does not leverage invariances only to have pseudo labels. It is known what is the objective in training and why it is helpful, e.g. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.10242.pdf. We do have theoretical results for generalization in invariant learning, see for instance https://openreview.net/pdf?id=HxeTEZJaxq.
2) The used definition of equivariance is not very common "some non-constant effect u". The effect u needs to be tied to the transformation t in the input. It is more rigorous to define a t as a group action and u as a the action of the same element in the group in the range of g. If the authors want to avoid being restricted to group transformations (which I believe is the case), they need to provide a more rigorous definition of equivariance. Also equivariance is not with respect to an object, as said in page 4, but to a transformation.
3) Due to presentation and clarity of the text, I was confused on whether the authors were training invariant and equivariant models or not. From what I understood no. Instead, they are evaluating the impact of a data augmentation procedure. To this end, I find it hard to understand the comparison of equiv and invariance. Equivariance is mostly used to then build invariant models, e.g. a middle step.
4) It's hard to follow why the proposed changes in data test equivariance: "a model’s representations change based
on features that should separate classes in a classification task (equivariance)".
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The sentences are quite long making it hard to follow the text. Also, it is not clear from start what is the goal of the paper, which makes it hard to understand. I recommend the authors give a direct description right on introduction. I believed you were testing invariant and equivariant models until half of the paper. There is novelty in the dataset proposed and since the dataset would be public, it seems as reproducible as possible for this case.
content.summary_of_the_review: Please, see the weaknesses part. I think this paper needs a lot of work in presentation. Further, the authors need to more formally describe the equivariance property and how their data selection strategy tests it. After these improvements, I recommend a submission to a dataset track.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful feedback and helpful suggestions! We will revise the paper to address the concerns that were raised.

### Connection to previous results on invariance
We agree that there is prior work studying invariance and equivariance as well as their implications for performance. The novelty of this paper lies in investigating the relative importance of these factors when transferring representations between tasks.
We acknowledge that this distinction currently is not clear enough. We will improve the work in this respect and also discuss the related work pointed out here as well as distinctions to our work.

### Clarity
We will work towards improving the clarity of the paper, especially regarding the goals and implications of the analysis as well as the role of the synthetic dataset in achieving these goals.

Please also see our general comment for other issues that we are planning to address based on the feedback here, especially also regarding changing the usage of the notion of equivariance used in the paper.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies how invariances are learned in a networks trained on classification tasks, and how those invariances help or hurt performance on related tasks. The paper approaches this question using a synthetic dataset, composed of prototype images superimposed on random backgrounds, where particular invariances can be parametrically varied (things like the rotation, scale, and translation of the prototype).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- Use of synthetic data allows for more controlled experiments on invariance.
- Collection of experiments is compelling and thorough.

Weaknesses
- Currently, the selected transformations are treated as an arbitrary set (with no distinction between different types of transformations). Given that some of the transformations are pretty different, it would be helpful to see more discussion about the different types of transformations that were studied, and how the results vary across them. For example, are the observed effects more pronounced for particular transformations (e.g. translation vs flips)?
- I would encourage the authors to release the synthetic dataset (set of 50,000 train/test/validation images) for the academic community to use/build off of.

Minor comments

- Figure 1: show examples of smoothly varying the transformation, for each transformation type.
- how finely do you sample the different transformations?
- are the results in Fig 2 dependent on particular transformations? Some are binary, others are continuous. Any differences there?
- Figure 3: error bars?
- Implication of Fig 3 is that the network is learning to be invariant to the distractor on the training task, which hurts the performance when the distractor becomes the target.
- typo in the last paragraph of Section 3.2: "extend" should be "extent"
- Fig. 5 might be better visualized as a heat map, with training datasets on one axis and transfer (evaluation) datasets on the other. That way, the diagonal would be close to 1, which is more intuitive than looking across colors. (You wouldn't be able to easily show the error bars, but I think that is worth the trade-off).
- Perhaps a point for discussion, but I'm curious about what these results say about unsupervised objectives, e.g. reconstruction in an auto encoder? There, the task demands that there are no invariances (since the full input needs to be reconstructed). Does that potentially explain why unsupervised pre-training often underperforms supervised pre-training on related tasks?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is, for the most part, clearly written. To the best of my knowledge, the work is original.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I really enjoyed reading this paper. I thought the use of the synthetic dataset was clever, and it led to a number of insights about the role of invariance and equivariance in learned representations. I would love to see some discussion about the different types of transformations, and if the various results are sensitive to particular transformations.

content.title: Thank you for your valuable feedback! We will include the suggestions in a future version of the paper.
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful feedback and helpful suggestions! We are delighted to see that the reviewer appreciates the ideas in this work! We will revise the paper to address the concerns that were raised.

### More careful characterization and examination of the set of transformations
We agree that a more careful categorization and examination of the set of transformations and their effects would be useful. We will explore which categorizations would be most useful, with potential separation criteria being the input properties that transformations change (geometry, color, etc.) or whether they are continuous or discrete.

### Releasing a dataset
We are planning to make all code public and reusable upon acceptance of the paper, including parts related to the synthetic dataset.
There are, however, many different variants of the Transforms-2D dataset depending on which permutation of transformations is used, so we believe that instead of releasing a static, CIFAR-like dataset with a fixed set of images, it will be more useful to release a generator that can be configured with the desired set of transformations and objects.

### Unsupervised objectives
The scope of our work is limited to learning non-injective functions that allow for invariance, so it is not directly applicable to certain unsupervised objectives with the goal of learning injective functions, such as image generation or reconstruction. However, the suggestion of studying whether the absence of (desirable) invariance in such tasks reduces their utility for pretraining representations that should later be used as the basis for non-injective functions (e.g. classification) is quite intriguing and we will explore this direction further.

Please also see our general comment for other issues that we are planning to address based on the feedback here.

content.title: We will improve the paper based on the valuable feedback we received but withdraw it for now.
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their feedback, constructive criticism and suggestions. They will be quite helpful to us in improving the work going forward.
Based on the comments made here, we believe that the work is not ready for publication yet. We will address the issues that were pointed out. However, this will take more time than what is available until the end of the discussion period, so we will withdraw the paper now.

We see the main areas of improvement for the paper as follows:

### Clarifying the main contributions of the paper
We see the main contribution of the paper in showing the *relative importance* of invariance compared to other factors when transferring representations from one task to another. We do so by leveraging a synthetic dataset that allows us to control which invariances a model possesses as well as which ones are required for a target task.
These contributions are currently not stated clearly enough, and we will improve the exposition of the paper in this regard.

### Providing better contextualization wrt. prior work on the importance of invariance
We thank the reviewers for pointing us to relevant related work and will review it in the paper. In particular, we will more clearly highlight and contrast the novel aspects of our work.

### Changing the current notion of equivariance
As pointed out by the reviewers, the definition of equivariance used in the paper is currently somewhat vague and used inconsistently in some places. We will either make it more formal and compliant with existing definitions or replace it with a term that is more suitable.

### Additional experiments
We will add further experiments that are inspired by the suggestions made here. In particular we will explore ways to validate the insights derived from the synthetic, controlled experiments on common real-world benchmarks and investigate the effect of pretraining tasks with the goal of learning injective functions that don’t allow for invariance (e.g. image reconstruction).
